title: Ancient Greeks Built A Working Computer 2,000 Years Ago
description:
A corroded lump of bronze pulled from a Greek shipwreck in 1901 turned out to be a working mechanical computer -- it tracked the sun, moon, and planets, and predicted eclipses. Nothing this advanced shows up again for roughly a thousand years.

#shorts #techfacts #antikythera #didyouknow
sources: History.com's "How the Secrets of an Ancient Greek 'Computer' Were Revealed"
National Hellenic Museum's "The World's Oldest Computer: The Antikythera Mechanism"
World History Encyclopedia's Antikythera Mechanism entry

scenes.text: In 1901, divers searching a Greek shipwreck pulled up a corroded lump of bronze that turned out to be a working computer -- built over two thousand years ago.
Inside were at least thirty interlocking gears, precisely cut to track the positions of the sun, moon, and planets, and to predict eclipses years in advance.
It even displayed which panhellenic games -- including the Olympics -- would be held in any given year, all from hand-turning a single crank.
Researchers only fully understood what it did decades later, using X-ray imaging to read inscriptions and gear patterns hidden inside the corroded bronze.
Nothing built with this level of precision shows up again in the historical record for roughly another thousand years.
One part of it even used a clever pin-and-slot gear design to mimic the moon's slightly uneven orbit -- something you wouldn't expect from a culture working entirely by hand, with no electricity.
Would you have guessed something this advanced existed two thousand years ago?
